specPoints.text: understand that mutation is a rare, random change in genetic material that can be inherited

primer.text: Short but load-bearing: the core definition of mutation, a rare and random alteration of the genetic material that offspring can receive, plus the two qualifiers exams attach to it — changes happen continuously, and most of them leave the protein effectively unchanged.

lessons.title: The Core Definition
lessons.opening: A mutation is a rare, random change in the base sequence of a gene or chromosome; it can be inherited, it happens continuously across generations, and most of the time the protein it codes for stays effectively unchanged.
keyPoints: Mutations are rare, random changes in genetic material.
They occur in the DNA base sequence of a gene or a chromosome.
Mutations can be inherited by offspring.
They happen continuously rather than in bursts.
In most cases the protein is untouched, or nudged so slightly that its function survives.

low.restatement: A mutation is a rare random DNA change, inheritable and mostly harmless.
low.analogy: An occasional wrong keystroke in a long manuscript that rarely spoils the story.
low.examPointer: Hit all four qualifiers: rare, random, inheritable, continuous.

medium.restatement: The base sequence dictates the amino acid sequence, so the protein changes only when the mutation reaches that far.
medium.analogy: A recipe change only matters if it alters an ingredient that the dish actually uses.
medium.examPointer: Pair this definition with the advanced note's effect ladder.

check.stem: Which three words describe a mutation in the taught definition?

options.text: Rare, random and in the genetic material
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Mutations are rare and undirected.
No planning or usefulness is implied.
Most are neither harmful nor visible.

options.text: In the DNA base sequence of a gene or chromosome
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Proteins are the products, not the site.
The genetic material is the target.
Membranes carry no base sequences.

check.stem: Can a mutation pass to the next generation?

options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Inheritance is built into the definition.
The rule is general.
Inheritance does not depend on the cause.

check.stem: What usually happens to the protein a mutated gene codes for?

options.text: It is unchanged, or changed so slightly its function survives
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Destruction is rare.
Improvement is rarer still.
No pigment change is implied.

check.stem: A base sequence changes by one letter in a body cell of a grandfather. Could his grandchild inherit it?

options.text: Only if the change occurred in a cell type that contributes to reproduction
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Body-cell changes do not reach the next generation.
Changes in gamete-forming cells can be inherited.
Skin cells do not form gametes.

check.stem: State the definition of mutation taught here.
check.modelAnswer: A mutation is a rare and random alteration of the genetic material, and it can pass to offspring.

check.stem: What determines whether a mutation changes a protein?
check.modelAnswer: The DNA base sequence determines the amino acid sequence, so changes in a gene can sometimes change the protein it codes for.

check.stem: Explain why the word random matters in the definition of mutation.
check.modelAnswer: No mechanism aims a mutation at a useful trait; changes strike the sequence without regard to benefit, which is why most are neutral and selection, not intent, decides what persists.

check.stem: A single plant in a crop field shows an unexpected leaf shape. State what likely happened in that plant's genetic material and whether the change can reach its seeds.
check.modelAnswer: A random mutation likely struck a gene in that plant, and if the change occurred in cells that form gametes, it can be inherited through the seeds.

glossary.definition: A rare and random alteration of the genetic material, which offspring can receive.
The order of bases along a gene or chromosome.
To receive genetic material from a parent.
